headline: Blowout Jobs Report Tests the Rate Rally
tileReason: The daily 30-year average slipped to 7.17% Thursday, but this morning's much stronger-than-expected jobs report nudged bond yields back up, which points to slightly higher lender pricing today.
takeaway:
Mortgage rates eased again Thursday. The daily 30-year average dipped 0.05% to 7.17%, its lowest since late September. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, out Thursday, fell to 7.18% from 7.24%, its third straight weekly drop.

Thursday's dip came from a stock sell-off and cheaper oil. Tech stocks kept sliding, and when investors sell stocks they often park money in bonds, which pushes yields down. The 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates tend to follow, ended Thursday near 4.83%, its lowest since September, and oil was on track for its biggest weekly drop since 2020.

This morning's jobs report was a big surprise. Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, roughly three times the 56,000 to 65,000 forecasters expected, and August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000. The unemployment rate dipped to 4.1% and hourly pay rose 0.4% for the month, a bit faster than expected.

Bond yields rose on the news, but only modestly. The 10-year yield climbed about 0.03% to 0.04% to roughly 4.87% after the report, so lenders are likely to price a little higher today, though not enough to undo the week's gains. Oil is down slightly again this morning, with Brent near $97.50, which helps limit the damage.

A December Fed hike looks more likely again. Futures markets, where traders bet on Fed decisions, put the odds of a quarter-point hike on Dec 9 at about 75% to 77% after the report, up from about 68% earlier this morning. A strong job market with faster pay growth is exactly what keeps the Fed worried about inflation.

Borrowers still have a cushion. The Optimal Blue conforming index, which tracks rates on loans borrowers actually locked, sat 2.22% above the 10-year Treasury on Nov 3, versus a long-run average of about 1.76%, so mortgage rates have room to improve if markets settle.

Next big test: Tuesday's October inflation report (Nov 10). Next week also brings large government bond sales, and the bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day.

fedOdds.title: Odds of a Fed hike on Dec 9
fedOdds.beforeLabel: Fri, Nov 6, before the jobs report

fedOdds.note: CME FedWatch showed about 77% after the report, up from about 68% earlier Friday morning and below the roughly 82% peak on Nov 4. LSEG data cited by Reuters put it near 75%. Either way, a hike is still seen as the most likely outcome.

drivers.title: Jobs report blows past forecasts
drivers.text: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, about three times what forecasters expected, the prior two months were revised up by 84,000, and pay rose 0.4%. A hot job market can keep wages and spending, and therefore inflation, elevated, so investors sold bonds and the 10-year yield rose about 0.03% to 0.04% this morning to near 4.87%.

drivers.title: Tech stock sell-off sends money into bonds
drivers.text: Technology stocks kept falling Thursday. When investors pull money out of stocks, some of it flows into bonds, which pushes yields down. That helped the daily 30-year average dip 0.05% to 7.17%. A rebound in stocks could reverse this support.

drivers.title: Oil heads for its biggest weekly drop since 2020
drivers.text: Brent crude was on track for a weekly drop of about 16% after the midterm results raised hopes of de-escalation with Iran. Cheaper oil lowers fuel and shipping costs and eases inflation worries. Ongoing tanker attacks near the Strait of Hormuz keep a floor under prices, so this support can fade quickly.

drivers.title: December Fed hike back near 75%-77%
drivers.text: Futures put the odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec 9 at about 75% to 77% after the jobs report, up from about 68% before it. When investors expect higher short-term rates, longer-term rates, including mortgages, have a harder time falling. Tuesday's inflation report is the next big input.

drivers.title: Mortgage rates still far above Treasuries
drivers.text: The Optimal Blue conforming index sat 2.22% above the 10-year Treasury yield on Nov 3, compared with a long-run average of about 1.76%. That wide gap is a cushion: if markets calm down, there is room for mortgage rates to improve even if Treasury yields stay put.

outlook.basis: Still close to a coin flip, now leaning slightly toward higher. Rates just reached their lowest level since late September, and this morning's strong jobs report makes a December Fed hike more likely (about 75% to 77%), with faster pay growth adding to inflation worries. In borrowers' favor: oil is having its biggest weekly drop since 2020, the tech stock slump is pushing money into bonds, and mortgage rates are unusually far above the 10-year Treasury (about 2.22% vs. a long-run average near 1.76%). Big swing events: Tuesday's October inflation report, next week's government bond sales, any news from Iran, and the Dec 4 jobs report.
outlook.caveat: This is professional judgment from 30+ years watching these markets, not a guarantee. One oil headline or data surprise can move rates a quarter point in a day.

talkingPoints.buyers: The daily 30-year average dipped to about 7.17% Thursday, its lowest since late September and down from roughly 7.5% in early October. This morning's much stronger-than-expected jobs report nudged bond yields back up, and Tuesday's inflation report could move rates either way, so it's worth talking with Stuart about how locking, a float-down option (which lets you take a lower rate if rates drop after you lock), or waiting would each fit your closing date.
talkingPoints.sellers: Rates have eased for three weeks, which helps affordability at the margin, but buyers are still stretched above 7%, and a strong economy could keep rates from falling much further. Realistic pricing, or a seller credit buyers can use to lower their rate, can help a home stand out.
talkingPoints.oneLiner: Mortgage rates just hit their lowest since September around 7.17%, but a blowout jobs report this morning is testing that rally; Tuesday's inflation report is next.
